chapter: Starting out in New York and Chicago
title: First mixed band and how Minton's worked as a hiring hall
summary: Horace's first mixed group was in New York in the forties; Minton's, run by Teddy Hill for union official Minton, was where you could pick up a band for a gig, like musicians on the Jimmy Ryan's corner.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: In your early band, like in Wilberforce, or shortly thereafter, did you ever have any whites in your band?

Not in Wilberforce. In fact, you know that's a good question that you ask. My first mixed group, believe it or not, was in New York City; I'll have to say (inaudible) that. Yes. In fact, we've got to go back now -- now, I think we're
coming into the forties, because I'm getting ready to bring up a place called Minton's.

Which -- a great band leader named Teddy Hill ran for a guy that owned it named Mr. Minton who was an official in the union at 802 in New York City. And Minton's, of course, was a hangout for all the musicians.

Black, white, red, green, anything. But great musicians hung out there, and if you ever wanted to get a quick band up for a one-nighter all you had to do was walk in Minton's with your pencil and your paper and the guys got their horns and 'Hey man, you workin' tomorrow night?' 'Are you workin' Saturday night?' 'No.' 'You got a gig for me,' you know, one of those things? Like what's that place down on Broadway in New York? Was it Ryan's? That restaurant where a lot of musicians would hang out in front?

Jimmy Ryan's? A lot of guys used to stand on the corner, they tell me, with a saxophone, the guy say, 'Oh, you're a saxophone player. I want a trumpet player.' 'Well, wait a minute, I live right upstairs, let me -- I play trumpet too, you know.' The guys would go get those things, you know. I remember the guys out of Fletcher's band would tell me these things, you know? And I remember them, sure
